learningObjectives.title: What a balanced equation tells you
Using the mole ratio for masses, volumes and concentrations

questions.q: Aluminium burns in oxygen to form aluminium oxide. Which equation for this reaction is correctly balanced?
options: Al(s) + O₂(g) → AlO₂(s)
2Al(s) + 3O(g) → Al₂O₃(s)
2Al(s) + 3O₂(g) → Al₂O₃(s)
4Al(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Al₂O₃(s)
optionWhy: A student who balances by changing a formula picks this. The atoms match, but AlO₂ is not aluminium oxide: the charges Al³⁺ and O²⁻ fix the formula as Al₂O₃. Only coefficients may be changed when balancing.

A student who writes oxygen as single atoms picks this. The atom counts match, but oxygen exists as O₂ molecules, so the equation must use O₂; with O₂ the balanced equation is 4Al(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Al₂O₃(s).
A student who reads 3O₂ as three oxygen atoms picks this. The coefficient multiplies the whole formula: 3O₂ contains 3 × 2 = 6 O atoms but Al₂O₃ contains only 3, so oxygen is not balanced.
Aluminium oxide is Al₂O₃ (ions Al³⁺ and O²⁻) and oxygen gas is O₂. 3O₂ supplies 6 O atoms, matching 2Al₂O₃, which contains 4 Al atoms, so 4Al. Check: 4 Al and 6 O on each side.
questions.explain: Aluminium oxide is Al₂O₃ (ions Al³⁺ and O²⁻) and oxygen gas is O₂. 3O₂ supplies 6 O atoms, matching 2Al₂O₃, which contains 4 Al atoms, so 4Al. Check: 4 Al and 6 O on each side.

questions.q: Hydrogen burns in oxygen, and the quantities are measured at room temperature and pressure: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l). Which statement about the quantities shown by this equation is correct?
options: The mass of H₂ that reacts is twice the mass of O₂ that reacts.
Every 2 mol of H₂ react with 1 mol of O₂ to form 2 mol of H₂O.
Every 2 dm³ of H₂ and 1 dm³ of O₂ react to form 2 dm³ of H₂O.
The amount of H₂O formed equals the total amount of H₂ and O₂ used.
optionWhy: A student who reads the coefficients as a mass ratio picks this. The ratio 2 : 1 is by amount. In mass, 2 mol H₂ is 4.04 g and 1 mol O₂ is 32.00 g, so far less hydrogen than oxygen reacts by mass.

The coefficients give the ratio of amounts in mol: 2 mol H₂ : 1 mol O₂ : 2 mol H₂O. Mass is conserved (4.04 g + 32.00 g = 36.04 g), but the amounts and masses of the individual substances are not in the same ratio.

A student who applies gas-volume ratios to every substance picks this. The 2 : 1 volume ratio holds for the two gases, but water forms as a liquid, H₂O(l); 2 mol of liquid water occupies only about 36 cm³.
A student who thinks that amount in mol is conserved, like mass, picks this. Atoms are conserved, but here 3 mol of reactant molecules form 2 mol of water molecules.
questions.explain: The coefficients give the ratio of amounts in mol: 2 mol H₂ : 1 mol O₂ : 2 mol H₂O. Mass is conserved (4.04 g + 32.00 g = 36.04 g), but the amounts and masses of the individual substances are not in the same ratio.

questions.q: Iron is produced by reducing iron(III) oxide with carbon monoxide: Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g). What is the maximum mass of iron that can be produced from 40.0 g of iron(III) oxide? A_r: O 16.00; Fe 55.85
optionWhy: A student who inverts the mole ratio divides by 2 instead of multiplying: n(Fe) = 0.2505 ÷ 2 = 0.1252 mol, and 0.1252 × 55.85 = 6.99 g. Each Fe₂O₃ contains two Fe atoms, so there must be more Fe (in mol) than Fe₂O₃, not less.

A student who multiplies the A_r of iron by its coefficient finds the correct n(Fe) = 0.5009 mol but then uses 2 × 55.85 = 111.70 g mol⁻¹, giving 56.0 g. The coefficient has already been used in the mole ratio; m = nM uses the molar mass of one Fe atom, 55.85 g mol⁻¹.

A student who reads the coefficients as a mass ratio doubles the mass of iron(III) oxide: 2 × 40.0 = 80.0 g. That would be more iron than the oxide contains; the 1 : 2 ratio applies to amounts in mol, not masses.

questions.q: Which statement describes the theoretical yield of a product in a reaction?
options: The mass of product actually obtained at the end of the experiment
The total mass of all the reactants put in, since mass is conserved
The mass of product calculated from the amount of the limiting reactant
The mass of product calculated from the reactant with the smaller number of moles
optionWhy: A student who confuses the two yields picks this. The mass actually obtained is the experimental yield; the theoretical yield is calculated, and the experimental yield is normally smaller.

A student who thinks that all the reactants turn into product picks this. Only the limiting reactant is used up and some excess reactant is left over; other products may also form, so the product mass is not the total mass of the reactants.
The theoretical yield is the maximum mass of product, calculated from the amount of the limiting reactant using the mole ratio and assuming complete reaction with no losses.

A student who compares amounts without the mole ratio picks this. The limiting reactant is not always the one present in the smaller amount: for 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂, 0.200 mol CO with 0.125 mol O₂ leaves carbon monoxide limiting.
questions.explain: The theoretical yield is the maximum mass of product, calculated from the amount of the limiting reactant using the mole ratio and assuming complete reaction with no losses.

questions.q: A student heats 2.70 g of aluminium in 8.51 g of chlorine and collects 7.60 g of aluminium chloride: 2Al(s) + 3Cl₂(g) → 2AlCl₃(s). What is the percentage yield of aluminium chloride? A_r: Al 26.98; Cl 35.45
optionWhy: A student who takes the reactant with fewer moles as limiting chooses aluminium (0.1001 mol < 0.1200 mol) and gets a theoretical yield of 0.1001 × 133.33 = 13.34 g, so 7.60 ÷ 13.34 × 100 = 57.0%. Aluminium needs 1.5 mol Cl₂ per mol, so chlorine runs out first.

A student who assumes that all of the reactants turn into product takes the theoretical yield as 2.70 + 8.51 = 11.21 g, giving 67.8%. Aluminium is in excess and some is left over, so the maximum mass of product is 10.67 g.

A student who compares the product with the mass of the limiting reactant divides 7.60 g by the 8.51 g of chlorine, giving 89.3%. The theoretical yield is a mass of aluminium chloride, which also contains aluminium: 0.08002 mol × 133.33 g mol⁻¹ = 10.67 g.

n(Al) = 0.1001 mol and n(Cl₂) = 0.1200 mol. Al would need 1.5 × 0.1001 = 0.1501 mol Cl₂, so Cl₂ is limiting. n(AlCl₃) = 0.1200 × 2/3 = 0.08002 mol, theoretical yield = 0.08002 × 133.33 = 10.67 g, and percentage yield = 7.60 ÷ 10.67 × 100 = 71.2%.
questions.explain: n(Al) = 0.1001 mol and n(Cl₂) = 0.1200 mol. Al would need 1.5 × 0.1001 = 0.1501 mol Cl₂, so Cl₂ is limiting. n(AlCl₃) = 0.1200 × 2/3 = 0.08002 mol, theoretical yield = 0.08002 × 133.33 = 10.67 g, and percentage yield = 7.60 ÷ 10.67 × 100 = 71.2%.
questions.working: n(Al) = 2.70 g ÷ 26.98 g mol⁻¹ = 0.1001 mol; n(Cl₂) = 8.51 g ÷ 70.90 g mol⁻¹ = 0.1200 mol. Al would need 3/2 × 0.1001 = 0.1501 mol Cl₂, but only 0.1200 mol is present, so Cl₂ is limiting. n(AlCl₃) = 2/3 × 0.1200 = 0.08002 mol. M_r(AlCl₃) = 26.98 + 3(35.45) = 133.33. Theoretical yield = 0.08002 mol × 133.33 g mol⁻¹ = 10.67 g. Percentage yield = 7.60 g ÷ 10.67 g × 100 = 71.2%.

questions.q: Hydrogen is manufactured by reacting methane with steam: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + 3H₂(g). In one batch, 16.0 kg of methane gave 4.80 kg of hydrogen. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen by this reaction? A_r: H 1.01; C 12.01; O 16.00
optionWhy: A student who leaves out the coefficient uses one H₂: 2.02 ÷ 34.07 × 100 = 5.93%. Each CH₄ gives three H₂ molecules, so the desired product counts as 3 × 2.02 = 6.06.

A student who uses the batch masses divides 4.80 kg by 16.0 kg to get 30.0%. Atom economy uses M_r values and coefficients from the balanced equation, so it does not depend on the masses used in a particular batch.

Atom economy = M_r(desired product) ÷ ΣM_r(all reactants) × 100, using the coefficients: 3 × 2.02 ÷ (16.05 + 18.02) × 100 = 6.06 ÷ 34.07 × 100 = 17.8%. The rest of the mass ends up as the by-product CO.
A student who leaves the steam out of the denominator uses M_r(CH₄) alone: 6.06 ÷ 16.05 × 100 = 37.8%. Every reactant in the equation counts: 16.05 + 18.02 = 34.07.
questions.explain: Atom economy = M_r(desired product) ÷ ΣM_r(all reactants) × 100, using the coefficients: 3 × 2.02 ÷ (16.05 + 18.02) × 100 = 6.06 ÷ 34.07 × 100 = 17.8%. The rest of the mass ends up as the by-product CO.
questions.working: M_r(CH₄) = 12.01 + 4(1.01) = 16.05; M_r(H₂O) = 2(1.01) + 16.00 = 18.02; M_r(H₂) = 2(1.01) = 2.02. Atom economy = [3 × M_r(H₂) ÷ (M_r(CH₄) + M_r(H₂O))] × 100 = (6.06 ÷ 34.07) × 100 = 17.8%. The batch masses are not needed: atom economy depends only on the stoichiometry of the equation.

questions.q: Which statement about atom economy and waste in an industrial process is correct?
options: The higher the percentage yield, the higher the atom economy, so less waste is produced.
Atom economy counts one molecule of each substance, so the coefficients do not affect it.
A process with an atom economy of 100% produces no waste of any kind at all.
The lower the atom economy, the greater the proportion of reactant mass that becomes waste.
optionWhy: A student who confuses atom economy with percentage yield picks this. Atom economy is fixed by the balanced equation; improving the yield does not change the proportion of the reactant mass that goes into by-products.

A student who leaves the coefficients out of the calculation picks this. The masses must match the balanced equation: coefficient × M_r for the desired product and for each reactant, so changing the coefficients changes the atom economy and the proportion of mass that becomes waste.

A student who treats atom economy as a complete measure of waste picks this. An atom economy of 100% means that the reaction forms no by-product, but unreacted reactants, side reactions and solvents can still create waste.

Atom economy is the percentage of the total mass of reactants that can end up in the desired product. The rest ends up in by-products, so as atom economy falls, the proportion of the reactant mass converted to waste rises: the two are inversely related.
questions.explain: Atom economy is the percentage of the total mass of reactants that can end up in the desired product. The rest ends up in by-products, so as atom economy falls, the proportion of the reactant mass converted to waste rises: the two are inversely related.
